title: What training does New York's Retail Worker Safety Act require?
seoTitle: NY Retail Worker Safety Act training
description: NY Retail Worker Safety Act: interactive violence prevention training at hire, then yearly or every two years, and panic buttons, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: New York's Retail Worker Safety Act, Labor Law section 27-e, requires employers with 10 or more retail employees in the state to adopt a workplace violence prevention policy and give interactive prevention training at hire. After that, employers with 50 or more retail employees train yearly, and smaller ones every two years. Training is on paid time with a written copy. Employers with 500 or more retail employees must provide silent response buttons from January 1, 2027.
keyTakeaways: Coverage: employers with 10 or more retail employees anywhere in New York State, counted across all store locations. Restaurants and other businesses that mainly sell food for on-site consumption are not retail stores under the Act.
Training frequency: at hire, then annually for employers with 50 or more retail employees, and every two years for those with fewer than 50.
Training must be interactive, delivered during paid work time, and accompanied by a written version in English and, where the Department of Labor has a translation, the employee's primary language.
Required content includes de-escalation, active shooter events, emergency procedures and exits, use of security alarms and emergency devices, and supervisor responsibilities.
From January 1, 2027, employers of 500 or more retail employees statewide must provide every retail employee with a silent response button and train them to use it.
regulator: New York State Department of Labor (NYSDOL), Safety, Health and Essential Rights (SHER) Program
appliesTo: Employers with 10 or more retail employees in New York State, counted across all locations
Employees working on-site at a retail store, including staff of contractors such as cleaning companies
Employers with 500 or more retail employees statewide (silent response buttons from January 1, 2027)

sections.heading: Who does the Retail Worker Safety Act apply to?

blocks.text: The Act applies to New York State employers with 10 or more employees working at a retail store or stores. The New York State Department of Labor's [Retail Worker Safety overview](https://dol.ny.gov/retail-worker-safety) states that retail stores "include any store that sells goods directly to the public at retail" and "do not include businesses that primarily sell food to be eaten on-site, such as restaurants."

The Department's [FAQs](https://dol.ny.gov/retail-worker-safety-act-frequently-asked-questions) clarify three counting rules. First, only retail employees count: an employer with seven retail staff and five marketing and administrative staff is not covered. Second, retail employees are counted across all New York locations, so five staff at each of two stores is enough. Third, employees of a cleaning business who work on-site at retail stores are covered, and their employer must provide the policy and training.

The Act is in [New York Labor Law section 27-e](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/LAB/27-E). For international retailers, coverage follows where the retail employees work, not where the company is headquartered. This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: How often must retail employers provide the training?

blocks.text: All covered employers must train at hire; after that, frequency depends on the number of retail employees. Section 27-e states that training "shall be provided to all retail employees upon hire and on an annual basis thereafter," and that employers "employing fewer than fifty retail employees shall provide such workplace violence prevention training upon hire and once every two years thereafter."

blocks.title: Check older guidance
blocks.text: The Department's printable [guidance overview (P766)](https://dol.ny.gov/retail-worker-safety-guidance-overview-p766) describes training "upon hire and annual thereafter" without the two-year option for smaller employers. The current statute text, the training page and the FAQs all state the every-two-years rule for employers with fewer than 50 retail employees, so the overview appears to predate that change.
The training must cover seven required areas set by the Act. The Department's [training page](https://dol.ny.gov/retail-workplace-violence-prevention-training) lists them as:

items: The requirements of the Retail Worker Safety Act.
Measures retail workers can take to protect themselves when faced with workplace violence.
Emergency procedures, emergency exits, and meeting places in the event of an emergency.
How to use security alarms or buttons and other worksite-specific emergency devices.

Responsibilities of supervisors and managers before, during, and after emergency situations, including developing worksite-specific emergency procedures and training on areas of previous security problems.

blocks.text: Employers can use the Department's free interactive model training or develop their own, which must meet the minimum requirements in section 27-e. The model training does not include store-specific information, so employers using it should add a worksite-specific list or map of emergency exits, the meeting location, instructions for emergency and security devices such as panic alarms, other store-specific procedures, and any history of security problems at the location.

sections.heading: What counts as interactive, and must training be paid?

blocks.text: Training is interactive if the employee provides input and receives a response, and it must take place during paid work time. The Department's FAQ states: "A training is considered interactive if it requires an employee to provide input during the training and the employee receives a response to the input they provide. Digital training can be considered interactive." In-person delivery is not required.

On pay, the FAQ answers an employee question directly: an employer may not require the training after work on unpaid time, because "Your employer must offer retail workplace violence prevention training during paid work time." At the time of training, employers must also provide a written version of the interactive training. The written template, and the policy, must be provided in English and in the employee's primary language if it is one of the languages for which the Department has published a translation.

The [policy page](https://dol.ny.gov/retail-workplace-violence-prevention-policy) adds that a reporting system for workplace violence incidents is a recommended best practice rather than a legal requirement, and the FAQ confirms that keeping incident records is recommended but not required. Both still make sense as inputs to training updates. See [how to design a compliance training program](/guides/how-to-design-a-compliance-training-program).

sections.heading: What do large retailers need to do by January 1, 2027?

blocks.text: Employers of 500 or more retail employees statewide must provide every retail employee with a silent response button from January 1, 2027, and train employees to use it. Section 27-e requires a button "to request immediate assistance from a security officer, manager, or supervisor while the employee is working at the employee's location in case of an emergency."

According to the FAQ, the button can be a physical button easily accessible in the workplace, a wearable device, or a mobile phone application. Mobile or wearable devices may only be installed on employer-provided equipment and may be used to track an employee's location only when the button is triggered. Training on the button should cover how to trigger it, who responds, and the location-tracking limits that apply to wearable and phone-based devices.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates the common content of a retail violence prevention course from each store's site-specific information, and links both to the roles and locations that need them. When a store's procedures or devices change, the affected people can be identified and retrained. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Does the Retail Worker Safety Act apply to restaurants?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Labor states that retail stores do not include businesses that primarily sell food to be eaten on-site, such as restaurants. A business that sells goods directly to the public at retail, such as a convenience store or drug store, is covered if it has 10 or more retail employees in New York.

faqs.q: Can an employer use only the state's model training?
faqs.a: Yes, but it should be supplemented. The model training is free and may be used by any covered employer, but it does not contain store-specific information. The Department advises adding emergency exits, meeting places, device instructions, store-specific procedures and any history of security problems at the location.

faqs.q: Does the training have to be in the employee's primary language?
faqs.a: The interactive training does not have to be delivered in the primary language. The employer must provide a written template of the training content, and the policy, in the employee's primary language if it is one of the languages for which the Department has published a translation, and in English otherwise.

faqs.q: Who enforces the Retail Worker Safety Act?
faqs.a: The New York State Department of Labor's Safety, Health and Essential Rights (SHER) Program handles complaints. Employees can file online, by email, or by mail, and complaints are kept anonymous where feasible. Retaliation against employees for raising workplace violence concerns is prohibited.
